cards.front: What does a stop sign at a railroad crossing require when no train is in sight?
cards.back: A stop sign at a railroad crossing means you must stop even when no train is visible.

cards.front: Which vehicles must stop at a crossing even with no stop sign or signal?
cards.back: Unless signs say otherwise, school buses, for-hire passenger vehicles, gasoline trucks and other vehicles hauling hazardous materials must stop and confirm no train is coming even without a stop sign or signal.

cards.front: What is a passive railroad crossing?
cards.back: Passive crossings have no flashing lights or gates; they rely on advance warning signs, pavement markings and crossbucks with yield or stop signs at or just before the tracks.

cards.front: How do you cross at a passive crossing?
cards.back: At a passive crossing, slow or stop as needed, yield to trains, check both directions, make sure every track is clear, and never race a train.

cards.front: How does an active crossing warn of a train?
cards.back: Active crossings warn of a train with some mix of gates, flashing lights, message signs, and bells or other sounds.

cards.front: How do passive and active crossings differ?
cards.back: Passive crossings use signs and markings only, while active crossings add gates, flashing lights or bells that announce a train.

cards.front: When must you stop at an active crossing?
cards.back: Stop whenever crossing bells ring, lights flash, or the gate is down or moving, and never drive through, around or under an activated crossing.

cards.front: After a train passes, when may you cross?
cards.back: After a train passes, wait until the gates rise, lights and bells stop, and you are sure all tracks are clear.

cards.front: What habits keep you safe while crossing tracks?
cards.back: Never stop on tracks, always expect a train, look both ways, and avoid changing gears while crossing.

cards.front: How should you cross tracks on a snowy road?
cards.back: On a snowy road, cross tracks with enough speed that you will not get stuck.

cards.front: When traffic is backed up past a crossing, when may you start across?
cards.back: When traffic may be backed up near a crossing, do not start across unless your vehicle can clear the far side of the tracks by at least six feet.

cards.front: How much warning do you get once crossing signals start?
cards.back: Once crossing lights and gates activate or you hear a train horn, you have about twenty seconds before the train arrives.

cards.front: What clearance and warning time apply at a busy crossing?
cards.back: You must clear the far side of the tracks by six feet before crossing into backed-up traffic, and you get only about twenty seconds of warning once the signals start.

cards.front: You are stuck on the tracks and a train is coming. What do you do?
cards.back: If you are stuck on the tracks and the gates are activated or a train is clearly coming, get everyone out and far from the tracks right away, then call nine one one.

cards.front: You are stuck on the tracks with no train or signals. What do you do?
cards.back: If stuck with no activated lights or gates and no train in sight, get everyone out and away, then call the railroad's number on the blue Emergency Notification Sign and report the crossing ID.

cards.front: What is on the crossing ID, and what can railroad officials do?
cards.back: The crossing ID on the Emergency Notification Sign has six digits and one letter; railroad officials may slow, stop or divert a train, and you then call nine one one.

cards.front: What does an Emergency Notification System sign give you?
cards.back: An Emergency Notification System sign at or near a grade crossing gives a phone number and the crossing's US DOT number for reporting emergencies or broken warning devices.

cards.front: When stuck on tracks, when do you call emergency services and when the railroad?
cards.back: If stuck on tracks with a train coming or gates down, get out and call nine one one; if no train is in sight and nothing is activated, get everyone out and call the railroad emergency number on the blue sign.

cards.front: What should you do every time you park?
cards.back: Whenever you park, turn off the engine, set the parking brake rather than trusting the transmission, take the keys and lock the vehicle.

cards.front: What should you check before opening your door?
cards.back: Before opening your door, watch for passing bicycles, motorcycles, mopeds and vehicles and check your mirrors.

cards.front: Why open the driver's door with your right hand?
cards.back: Opening the driver's door with your right hand turns you to look over your left shoulder for oncoming cyclists and pedestrians.

cards.front: Which way should you face walking back to the driver's side?
cards.back: Walk back to the driver's side facing oncoming traffic.

cards.front: Which way do you turn your wheels parking on a hill?
cards.back: Parking downhill, turn the wheels toward the curb; parking uphill, turn them away from the curb; with no curb, turn them so the vehicle will not roll into traffic.

cards.front: Why set the parking brake on a hill?
cards.back: Always set the parking brake on a hill, because the transmission is not built to act as a brake.

cards.front: How do wheel positions differ for downhill and uphill parking?
cards.back: Wheels turn toward the curb when parked downhill and away from the curb when parked uphill.

cards.front: How do you start a parallel park?
cards.back: To parallel park, choose a space on the passenger side, signal, check mirrors, and pull alongside the car ahead of the space leaving two to five feet between you.

cards.front: How do you begin backing into a parallel space?
cards.back: Brake, shift to reverse, check traffic behind, then back slowly while checking mirrors and looking over your right shoulder.

cards.front: How do you steer while backing into a parallel space?
cards.back: Turn the wheel right as you start backing to angle the rear in, then turn the other way once the rear is mostly in, making an S turn that straightens the car.

cards.front: How do you finish a parallel park?
cards.back: Center the car in the space, park no more than six to twelve inches from the curb, and check traffic before opening your door.

cards.front: What are the two distances in a parallel park?
cards.back: When parallel parking, pull up two to five feet beside the car ahead, and finish no more than six to twelve inches from the curb.

cards.front: Can someone without a cane or wheelchair be entitled to a disability space?
cards.back: Disabilities are not always visible, so someone without a cane or wheelchair may still be entitled to a disability space.

cards.front: What gives free parking to a vehicle with a disability placard?
cards.back: Free parking is given only to vehicles showing a disability placard with a yellow free-parking sticker, which has stricter rules than a disability plate or placard.

cards.front: Who may use a disability parking space?
cards.back: To use a disability space, you or your passenger must have a qualifying disability, such as blindness or a temporary or permanent condition that greatly limits walking or needs an assistive device, plus a disability plate or placard.

cards.front: When should you not use a disability space even with a placard?
cards.back: Do not use a disability space if no occupant is disabled or the disabled person is not going into the store with you.

cards.front: Why must you keep off the striped area of a van-accessible space?
cards.back: Van-accessible spaces are wider to fit a wheelchair lift and ramp, so never park on their blue-striped area or block ramps and curb cuts.

cards.front: What does a disability plate or placard allow, and what does the yellow sticker add?
cards.back: A disability plate or placard lets you use a disability space, but only a placard with the yellow sticker gives free parking.

cards.front: Can local parking rules be stricter than state law?
cards.back: Local parking ordinances may be stricter than state law, with signs posted at city limits.

cards.front: Who pays a ticket for an illegally parked vehicle?
cards.back: The owner of an illegally parked vehicle pays the ticket, or the person leasing it if the vehicle is leased.

cards.front: Where do posted signs or emergencies forbid parking?
cards.back: Never park where no stopping, no standing or no parking signs are posted, or within five hundred feet of a fire or crash.

cards.front: Which doorways and views must you never block when parking?
cards.back: Do not park in front of a driveway, alley, theater, emergency exit or fire escape, or where you block the view of drivers turning at an intersection.

cards.front: How far from the curb, and facing which way, may you park?
cards.back: Never park more than twelve inches from the curb or facing against traffic.

cards.front: Where on bridges, tunnels and highways may you not park?
cards.back: Do not park on or under a bridge unless posted, on an overpass or in a tunnel, and outside city or village limits do not park in a highway lane when there is a shoulder.

cards.front: Which walkways and lanes must you never park on?
cards.back: Do not park on a sidewalk, in front of a public or private driveway, or inside an intersection, crosswalk or marked bike lane.

cards.front: Which other parking acts are illegal?
cards.back: Double parking beside a legally parked vehicle, blocking a rural mailbox, and parking at a transit stop are all illegal.

cards.front: Who receives a parking ticket for a leased car?
cards.back: A parking ticket goes to the vehicle's owner, or to the person leasing it if the vehicle is leased, not simply to whoever parked it.

cards.front: How far must you park from a fire hydrant?
cards.back: Never park within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant.

cards.front: How far must you park from a fire station driveway?
cards.back: Keep twenty feet from a fire station driveway on your side of the street, and seventy-five feet from it on the opposite side when marked.

cards.front: How far must you park from a railroad crossing?
cards.back: Never park within fifty feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing.

cards.front: How far must you park from a stop sign or traffic light?
cards.back: Keep at least thirty feet away from a stop sign, traffic light or flashing beacon when parking, and the same applies to a warning sign.

cards.front: How far must you park from a crosswalk or a plain intersection?
cards.back: Stay twenty feet from a marked crosswalk, or fifteen feet from an intersection that has no crosswalk.

cards.front: Which parking distance goes with a hydrant, a fire station driveway, a stop sign and a rail?
cards.back: Parking distances differ by object: fifteen feet from a hydrant, twenty feet from a fire station driveway on your side, thirty feet from a stop sign or signal, and fifty feet from the nearest rail.

cards.front: How does the fire station driveway distance change across the street?
cards.back: A fire station driveway needs twenty feet of clearance on the same side of the street but seventy-five feet on the opposite side when that distance is marked.

cards.front: How do the crosswalk and plain-intersection distances differ?
cards.back: Parking near a crosswalk requires twenty feet, but near an intersection without a crosswalk the gap is fifteen feet.

recap_hooks.text: Stop at a crossing stop sign, and certain buses and hazmat vehicles stop at every crossing.
Passive crossings use signs and markings; active ones add gates, lights and bells.
Stop for bells, lights or gates, and wait after the train until every track is clear.
Never stop on tracks; cross only if you can clear the far side, since warnings give about twenty seconds.
Stuck on the tracks, get everyone out and away first, then call.
The blue sign gives the railroad number and the crossing ID to report.
Engine off, parking brake, keys, lock, and look before you open the door.
Downhill wheels toward the curb, uphill away.
Pull alongside, back slowly in an S turn, and finish centered close to the curb.
A qualifying disability and a plate or placard allow a disability space; the yellow sticker adds free parking.
Keep off van-accessible stripes, and skip the space if no disabled person is going in.
Obey posted signs, keep driveways and exits clear, and park close to the curb facing with traffic.
The owner, or the lessee, pays the ticket.
Fifteen from a hydrant, twenty from a fire station driveway, thirty from signs and signals, fifty from the rail.
Twenty feet from a crosswalk, fifteen from a plain intersection.
